subtype: Catching the mood of a parent [Receiver]
passage: The evening before Eid, Ammi chopped onions fast in the small Lucknow flat, her lips pressed tight. She checked the clock, then her phone, then the clock again. Nobody said anything was wrong. Wasim stopped driving his toy bus round the table leg and came to stand against her. When Ishita from next door knocked to call him down to the swings, Wasim shook his head and gripped Ammi's kurta. 'What happened, jaan?' Ammi asked. His eyes filled. 'I don't know,' he whispered. Ammi put the knife down, breathed out slowly, and picked him up.

qa.q: What was Ammi chopping the evening before Eid?
qa.a: Ammi was chopping onions.

qa.q: Why did Wasim grip Ammi's kurta and refuse the swings?
qa.a: He had picked up Ammi's tension and felt uneasy and clingy himself, even though no one had said anything was wrong.

qa.q: What could Ammi do when she sees her mood rubbing off on Wasim?
qa.a: She can do what she started to: stop, breathe out, hold him, and tell him simply that she is a bit busy getting ready for Eid but he is safe.

qa.q: How might Ishita see Wasim's refusal at the door?
qa.a: Ishita might be puzzled, because from the doorway nothing looks wrong; Ishita can't see the tension Wasim has caught from Ammi.

grounding: Shows a young child sensing a parent's unspoken tension before a festival and becoming clingy and tearful without knowing why.

subtype: Laughter and panic in a class [Actor]
passage: Two days before the Losar holidays, the Class 5 room in Gangtok smelled of the khapse someone had brought from home. Then Vinita burst in from the corridor. 'The maths test is tomorrow, not after the holidays! Someone in 5B said!' In a minute the room had changed. Tsering was flipping through his notebook. Two girls by the window looked close to tears. Dolma felt her stomach go tight, though the news had come only from Vinita, and Vinita hadn't heard it from a teacher. She pulled out her fractions notes with shaking fingers. When Ma'am Lhamu came in and heard the noise, she laughed. 'Who told you that? The test is still on the fourteenth.' The whole room breathed out at once, and somebody started to giggle.

qa.q: Who first brought the news that the test was tomorrow?
qa.a: Vinita burst in from the corridor with it.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she pulled out her fractions notes?
qa.a: Dolma felt anxious and swept into the panic, even though she knew the news had not come from a teacher 😰

qa.q: What could Dolma do the next time a rumour like this sweeps the class?
qa.a: She could pause and ask where the news came from, then check with the teacher before letting the worry take over.

qa.q: How might Ma'am Lhamu see the class when she walks in?
qa.a: Because she knows the real date, the panic looks funny to her, and she can see how fast one unchecked story set the whole room worrying.

grounding: Shows worry from an unchecked rumour about a test spreading through a class faster than the facts, until the teacher corrects it.

subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
passage:

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do when the whole stand started chanting?
qa.a: Ujjwal went with it, standing on the bench and yelling at the ref.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal feel about the night now, and what shows it?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels a mix of joy and embarrassment: the hug and the jumping were wonderful, but the anger at the ref wasn't really Ujjwal's own, hence the plan to apologise to coach.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal try at the next match to keep the warm part without the yelling?
qa.a: Notice the moment a chant starts, ask 'do I actually think that?', and cheer for the team instead of joining in against the ref.

grounding: Shows a teenager swept up in a crowd's joy and anger at a match, sharing warm moments but also acting in an unusual way.

subtype: Setting the tone of a team [Response]
passage: By Wednesday of release week, Joseph noticed the pattern. He had snapped at the tester on Monday; by Tuesday the whole team was snapping at each other, and Aditi, usually the first to flag a bug, had gone silent in the standups, her camera off. That evening he scrolled back through the team chat and saw his own message: 'Why is this STILL broken?' He winced. On Thursday, before walking into the glass meeting room on the fourth floor of the Koramangala office, he stood by the water cooler and took three slow breaths. 'Okay,' he began, keeping his voice low. 'This release is tight, and I've been short with all of you. That's on me, not you. Let's just list what's stuck.' There was a pause. Then Aditi spoke. 'The payment screen crashes on older phones. I found it on Monday. I didn't want to be the one to say it.'

qa.q: What message of his own did Joseph find in the team chat?
qa.a: He found 'Why is this STILL broken?'

qa.q: Why did Joseph wince when he read his own message?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and uneasy, seeing that his irritation had spread through the team and made people like Aditi stop speaking up.

qa.q: Which of Joseph's steps settled the room, and why?
qa.a: Taking slow breaths, speaking low and naming both the pressure and his own shortness; owning the tension made it feel safe for others to talk 👍

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi during the snappish days?
qa.a: Aditi felt it wasn't safe to bring bad news, so she sat on a crash she had found on Monday until Joseph's calm made speaking up possible.

grounding: Shows a young team lead noticing his stress spreading through the team, then calming himself and admitting the pressure honestly, which settles the group.

subtype: Being known as fair or a cheat [Actor]
passage:
'Sharmila, you're in? Good, you count fair,' said Rohan, drawing a circle in the dust behind Block C.
'Can I play too?' Nitin asked.
'We've got enough,' said Rohan.
'You had five people yesterday. Now you have four.'
Tanu looked at the ground. 'Yesterday you nudged your marble when I turned to watch the rockets.'
'That was a joke!'
'And on Dhanteras you said you'd give back Rohan's blue one if you lost. You lost.'
Nitin's ears went hot. He dug in his pocket and held out the blue marble. 'Here. Sorry.'
Rohan took it and said nothing.
Sharmila glanced from one to the other. 'Maybe tomorrow?'
'Maybe,' said Rohan. Nitin sat on the steps and watched the Diwali holiday game go on without him.

qa.q: What did Nitin hand back to Rohan?
qa.a: Nitin held out the blue marble.

qa.q: What does Nitin's ears going hot suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and ashamed once the others say the nudged marble and the broken promise out loud.

qa.q: What could Nitin do over the next games to be trusted again?
qa.a: Play fair and keep every promise, even small ones, again and again, because one apology won't erase what the others remember.

qa.q: Why might Sharmila be welcomed when Nitin is not?
qa.a: Sharmila is known for counting fair, so the others trust Sharmila; about Nitin they remember the nudged marble and the unpaid promise.

grounding: Shows a child who cheated and broke a promise at marbles being quietly left out, while a fair player is invited in.

passage:
'You didn't tell anyone,' Dhruv said, as the dhol started up again on the society lawn. It was the ninth night of Navratri.
'Tell anyone what?'
'About the garba. That I've been practising the steps in my room with the door locked.'
Vaibhav shrugged. 'You asked me not to.'
'In Class 7 I told Kabir I still slept with the light on. By lunch the whole class knew.' Dhruv pulled at his kurta sleeve. 'I still don't talk to him.'
'That was two years ago.'
'Yeah. Well.' Dhruv watched the dancers circle. 'So I told you a small thing first. On the first night. To see.'
'A test?' Vaibhav laughed. 'Did I pass?'
'You passed.' Dhruv took a breath. 'Papa might be moving to Pune for work. I haven't told anyone.'
Vaibhav stopped laughing. 'Okay. I'm listening.'

qa.q: What small thing did Dhruv tell Vaibhav on the first night?
qa.a: That he had been practising the garba steps in his room with the door locked.

qa.q: What is Dhruv feeling when he brings up Kabir?
qa.a: He still feels hurt and wary, because Kabir spread a private thing to the whole class two years ago, and that one breach has stayed with him.

qa.q: Was Dhruv's small test a sensible way to build a new friendship? Why?
qa.a: Yes; sharing something minor first let him check that Vaibhav kept it private before risking something that really mattered, like the news about Papa.

qa.q: If you were Vaibhav, how might it feel to learn you had been tested?
qa.a: Maybe a bit surprised at first, which is why Vaibhav laughs, but then glad to be trusted, and ready to take the bigger news seriously 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager testing a new friend with a minor secret, still wary after an old breach, before trusting them with something bigger.

passage: The week before Christmas, while his hostel room in Pune was strung with paper stars, Francis sent Naveen his marketing project draft. 'Just to see the format,' Naveen had said. 'I'm totally lost.' In January the professor called them both in. Whole paragraphs of Naveen's report matched Francis's, down to a typo in the third table. Naveen stared at the floor and said nothing. Francis walked back to the hostel feeling stupid more than angry. He had believed every word. That night his roommate Aby asked to see his notes for the statistics exam. Francis's first thought was no, not to anyone, ever again. Instead he pulled his chair over, opened the notebook, and they worked through the problems together at the desk. He just didn't send the file.

qa.q: What matched between Naveen's report and Francis's?
qa.a: Whole paragraphs matched, down to a typo in the third table.

qa.q: How did Francis feel walking back to the hostel, and why?
qa.a: He felt betrayed and gullible, more stupid than angry, because he had believed Naveen's 'just to see the format' completely.

qa.q: How did Francis change the way he trusts, and why was that wise?
qa.a: He still helped Aby, but by working through the notes together instead of sending the file; that is careful trust rather than trusting nobody.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Aby if Francis had refused outright?
qa.a: Aby, who had done nothing wrong, would have been shut out and confused, paying for someone else's betrayal.

grounding: Shows a student whose shared draft is copied, who feels betrayed and gullible, and who then trusts more carefully instead of refusing everyone.

passage: On Trisha's third day at the shipping office in Kolkata, the monsoon knocked out the power at noon. The lifts stopped, the laptops died, and six people crowded into the pantry by the one window with any light. With nothing to do, they talked. 'Need a customs file by Friday? Ask Yusuf,' said Moumita. 'He'll say Thursday and hand it over Wednesday.' Someone laughed. 'Unlike Pranab. Pranab says yes to everything, then goes missing.' Trisha hadn't met either of them. She tucked the names away anyway, a little uneasy at how fast the verdicts came. Twenty minutes later a man with a torch appeared at the pantry door. 'Generator's on in ten. I've already told the clients we'll be late.' He was gone before she could ask his name. 'That,' said Moumita, 'was Yusuf.'

qa.q: What did Moumita say Yusuf does with a Friday deadline?
qa.a: He'll say Thursday and hand it over Wednesday.

qa.q: What did Trisha feel as the others handed out their verdicts?
qa.a: Trisha felt a little uneasy at how fast the judgements came, yet curious enough to tuck the names away.

qa.q: What could Trisha take from this for her own start at the office?
qa.a: That people are judged on small, repeated things like deadlines and follow-through, so being steady from the first week matters, while still checking pantry verdicts against her own experience.

qa.q: What does this pantry talk mean for Yusuf, who isn't there to hear it?
qa.a: His small habits, early files and warning clients during a power cut, have already built a reputation that reaches newcomers like Trisha before he meets them.

grounding: Shows a new employee hearing colleagues pass on who can and cannot be relied on before she has worked with them, and then seeing one small reliable act.

passage: Second chances? I've got one, and it isn't pretty. I'm Ramesh, and two years ago I kept saying 'almost done' on the warehouse software module when I hadn't started. Three times. My lead, Rekha, found out when the client called. I remember the silence on that call more than anything. The next morning I went to her desk and said it straight: 'I told you it was nearly done. It wasn't. I lied, and I'm sorry.' No excuses about workload. Then I stayed that weekend and built the module. I thought that would fix it. It didn't. For months she checked everything I sent. That stung, honestly. But I kept delivering on time, small things, boring things, week after week, and I never asked her if we were okay. Around the eighth month she gave me the new client without a second look. That's how it came back. Not with the apology. With the months.

qa.q: How did Rekha find out the module wasn't done?
qa.a: Rekha found out when the client called.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel during the months Rekha checked everything?
qa.a: Ramesh felt stung by it, yet accepted it without asking for quick forgiveness and kept delivering on time.

qa.q: Which step rebuilt the trust in the end, and why?
qa.a: Not the apology or the one weekend, but months of on-time work; that repeated evidence gave Rekha a reason to rely on Ramesh again.

qa.q: Why might Rekha have kept checking everything even after the apology?
qa.a: She had been told 'almost done' three times and found out through the client, so one apology couldn't show it wouldn't happen again; only a steady record could.

grounding: Shows a person who let a colleague down admitting it plainly, making amends and staying reliable for months until trust slowly returned.
